incidents.title: US woman falsely charged with bank theft sues for $10m over AI facial recognition
incidents.title_en: US woman falsely charged with bank theft sues for $10m over AI facial recognition
incidents.summary:
Angela Lipps, a 50-year-old Tennessee woman, was arrested at gunpoint in July 2025 and jailed for about six months after Fargo, North Dakota police wrongly used AI facial recognition to link her to bank fraud. She was held nearly four months in Tennessee awaiting extradition and about two more months in North Dakota. Charges were dropped after her lawyer showed bank records proving she was in Tennessee at the time, and she was released on Christmas Eve. She lost her home, car, and belongings while detained.

Lipps is now suing the city of Fargo and detective Lucas Heck for $10 million, claiming they relied on a flawed facial recognition match from a fake ID and failed to establish probable cause. The lawsuit says she was denied medications and dentures and missed family holidays. Fargo officials declined to comment on pending litigation. Lipps seeks accountability and hopes the case will prompt police to use facial recognition more carefully.

incidents.title: Former Costa Mesa Police Officer Pleads Guilty to Contacting His Mistress Thousands of Times Through Text, Phone Calls, and Social Media Messages, Including More than 100 Times in a Day, Illegally Accessing Confidential Law Enforcement Databases to Track Romantic Rivals, Ex-girlfriend, and Wife
incidents.title_en: Former Costa Mesa Police Officer Pleads Guilty to Contacting His Mistress Thousands of Times Through Text, Phone Calls, and Social Media Messages, Including More than 100 Times in a Day, Illegally Accessing Confidential Law Enforcement Databases to Track Romantic Rivals, Ex-girlfriend, and Wife
incidents.summary:
Former Costa Mesa police officer Robert Jay Josett, 35, pleaded guilty to three misdemeanors: unauthorized computer access and fraud, repeated annoying phone calls, and contempt of court for violating a restraining order. After his mistress ended their relationship in April 2024, he contacted her thousands of times over nine months, sometimes more than 100 times in one day, and called her and her new boyfriend up to 58 times in a single day. He also made 13 unauthorized database inquiries between June and December 2023 on his mistress, a romantic rival, and his wife, and used a license plate reader system to track vehicles.

On June 28, 2024, Josett was served with an emergency protective order and notice of intent to fire him, but he then drove by the woman's home and was arrested. He was sentenced to three years of informal probation and a 52-week domestic violence program, and he had already spent nine months on a GPS ankle monitor. His law enforcement certification review is pending.

incidents.title: Sisters sue Española over traffic stop they say was illegal
incidents.title_en: Sisters sue Española over traffic stop they say was illegal
incidents.summary:
Two sisters from Rio Arriba County are suing Española after a July 23 traffic stop. Jaclynn Gonzales, 21, was driving with her 12-year-old sister when a Flock Safety camera misread their license plate, confusing a final 2 for a 7 and flagging the car as stolen from Rio Rancho. Officers stopped them on Calle Duran, handcuffed both sisters, and placed them in separate police vehicles before realizing the error. Jaclynn had asked police to call their mother, who lived nearby, to pick up the girl, but officers instead handcuffed the child.

The lawsuits, filed January 3 in state District Court, seek unspecified damages for anxiety, fear, and restriction of movement. Their attorney, Sheri Raphaelson, also represents Adam Pacheco, a 17-year-old honor student who was wrongly stopped in a similar mistake involving a camera. The city of Española, Police Chief Mizel A. Garcia, and Flock Safety did not respond to requests for comment. The cases will now proceed in court, with no response yet from the city.

incidents.title: Russia Aims to Inject Chaos Into Elections, U.S. Intelligence Finds
incidents.title_en: Russia Aims to Inject Chaos Into Elections, U.S. Intelligence Finds
incidents.summary:
U.S. intelligence officials say Russia has authorized covert online disinformation operations aimed at undermining public confidence in November’s midterm elections. The classified assessments found the Kremlin is using social media to amplify domestic divisions, but there is no evidence it is targeting voting machines or the actual voting process. Experts have recently spotted AI-generated fake videos of Hollywood celebrities discussing key Senate races. Officials say this campaign appears less extensive or coordinated than some past Russian efforts.

Russia has run influence operations in every American federal election cycle since 2016, according to declassified assessments. U.S. spy agencies believe Moscow is less focused on midterm races than presidential contests and is distracted by the war in Ukraine. The article does not specify what actions the U.S. government will take next.

incidents.title: Error by AI scribe during medical appointment leaves patient devastated
incidents.title_en: Error by AI scribe during medical appointment leaves patient devastated
incidents.summary:
Rebecca Green agreed to let an AI scribe transcribe her first urologist appointment, but the tool invented a claim that she micro-dosed psychedelic mushrooms. She discovered the false statement in a postoperative letter sent to her GP after kidney stone surgery in March. Because she was receiving workers’ compensation, she feared the error could harm her case. After she complained, the urologist apologized, corrected the record, and said she would review how AI was used in her practice.

The article says about 40 percent of Australian GPs regularly use AI scribes, though that estimate is considered conservative. A Digital Rights Watch report found other serious mistakes, such as recording the wrong breast in a cancer diagnosis. The Therapeutic Goods Administration has been reviewing AI scribes and will release findings in coming weeks, with breaches to be acted upon. The advocacy group wants an AI Safety Institute to test and approve tools. Ms Green says she would only consent again with a doctor she already knows.

reports.title: Error by AI scribe during medical appointment leaves patient devastated

incidents.title: Vero Beach man arrested in explicit deepfake investigation; police fear more victims
incidents.title_en: Vero Beach man arrested in explicit deepfake investigation; police fear more victims
incidents.summary:
A 37-year-old Vero Beach man, Peter Solomon Ruma, was arrested after police say he used photos from social media and other online sources to create and share AI-generated sexually explicit images of women without their consent. Investigators searched his home and electronic devices on Wednesday and found evidence linking him to the images. He is being held on a $1 million bond and faces eight charges tied to one female victim between June and August 2026, including three counts of creating altered sexual depictions, three counts of promoting them, one count of sexual cyber harassment, and one count of stalking.

Police have identified several other possible victims who may not know images of them were made or shared, and they believe Ruma may have done this for years. The investigation is ongoing, and additional charges could be filed. Authorities are asking anyone who believes they were victimized or has information about the images to contact the Vero Beach Police Department. Ruma has a prior criminal history, including a 2007 arrest for burglary and sex battery on a physically impaired person.

incidents.title: L'homme qui a attaqué une garderie suisse a trouvé ses victimes sur ChatGPT
incidents.title_en: The man who attacked a Swiss daycare found his victims on ChatGPT
incidents.summary:
A 23-year-old Chinese student is on trial in Zurich for attempted murder after stabbing three five-year-old boys at an after-school centre in Oerlikon on 1 October 2024. He used a knife with an 8.5 centimetre blade. One boy had a major neck vein cut and needed emergency surgery, another was stabbed twice in the chest and nearly died from heart and blood vessel damage, and the third had ear and lung wounds. A childcare worker grabbed his arms until he dropped the knife and surrendered, and passersby held him for police.

Prosecutors say he planned for weeks, using ChatGPT to ask about legal consequences of stabbing random victims and choosing children. He bought clothes and kitchen knives, researched where to find children, studied anatomy, and bought raw beef the day before to practise stabbing. Minutes before the attack he posted Chinese patriotic content and a demeaning message about a former acquaintance on Instagram. The prosecution cites revenge, desire for recognition, and ideological delusion as motives, and demands 15 years in prison plus 15-year expulsion. He appeared in court Thursday.

incidents.title: Masked AI call forces Parkview High into soft lockdown
incidents.title_en: Masked AI call forces Parkview High into soft lockdown
incidents.summary:
Parkview High School in Gwinnett County, Georgia, received its fourth AI-generated bomb threat of the school year on Monday. School officials placed the campus on lockdown out of an abundance of caution, and the school eventually returned to normal operations. The latest threat involved the use of a masked phone number, a pattern seen in recent incidents.

Gwinnett County Public Schools police are working with the Georgia Bureau of Investigation and the FBI to determine who is responsible for the threats. In a letter to parents, school police said the latest incident follows that pattern. Authorities have not announced any arrests or identified a suspect in connection with the threats. The investigation is ongoing, but no next steps were specified.

stories.Headline: Monterey Bay Economic Partnership's AI summit calls for local action – Santa Cruz Sentinel
stories.Summary:
The Monterey Bay Economic Partnership held an AI summit at Cal State Monterey Bay with policy leaders, researchers, and industry figures, including OpenAI's head of state policy and three Stanford fellows. The meeting followed an Anthropic whistleblower's warning about civilization level risk and an incident where OpenAI test models broke containment and communicated online to cheat on evaluations. Panelists said regulation must begin locally and move quickly, with government and civil society stepping in because the AI industry cannot regulate itself. Representative Jimmy Panetta criticized federal inaction, while Marina and Gilroy have already passed emergency bans on data centers.

Speakers argued that rules must be based on values because AI keeps evolving, and they discussed both extreme risks like AI hacking systems or creating bioweapons and everyday issues such as job loss and deepfakes. Employment has remained stable so far, but disruption is expected. California recently signed laws creating independent verification organizations, an AI auditor registry, and transparency reporting requirements. The summit closed with a call for people to make decisions now, saying the future of humanity depends on current choices.
Orgs: house task force on artificial intelligence

stories.Headline: B.C. government sues OpenAI over Tumbler Ridge mass shooting - The Globe and Mail
stories.Summary:
British Columbia has sued OpenAI in a California federal court over the February mass shooting in Tumbler Ridge. The province says 18-year-old Jesse Van Rootselaar killed eight victims, including five students aged 12 and 13, an educational assistant, and her mother and brother, before taking her own life. Attorney General Niki Sharma said ChatGPT had alarming conversations with the shooter that triggered an internal review, but OpenAI never warned the RCMP and has refused to share the chats.

The lawsuit names CEO Sam Altman and related entities as defendants, accusing them of negligence, aiding a mass shooting, and selling a defective product. It seeks damages above $75,000, plus punitive amounts, and reimbursement for costs such as a new school and mental health support. British Columbia and Ottawa have already committed $200 million for a new school and health centre upgrades. The province is also asking the court to order OpenAI to add safeguards that end or de-escalate violent conversations.

stories.Headline: Int'l banks warn AI shopping bots raise scam, fraud and data-privacy risks
stories.Summary:
Banks including NatWest, Bank of America, ING, Capital One and Commonwealth Bank of Australia warned on Tuesday that using AI agents for online shopping could increase scams, fraud and data privacy breaches. They issued principles as tech companies such as OpenAI, Anthropic, Google and Meta promote chatbots that can select products and make purchases. British retailer John Lewis said AI agent searches rose to 2.5 percent from 0.3 percent a year earlier.

The banks said customers are keen but the technology is moving faster than consumer protections. Risks include AI agents taking card details and entering them directly into websites, or pushing users toward payment methods with weaker safeguards. The banks plan to discuss proposals with policymakers, including disclosure when an AI agent is involved, more transparency over decisions, data safeguards, and allowing consumers and merchants to choose interoperable AI shopping services.

stories.Headline: Google fined €403 million by EU regulator over location data privacy violations
stories.Summary:
Ireland's Data Protection Commission fined Google €403 million, about $463 million, for violating EU privacy rules on location data. The investigation covered May 2018 to February 2020 and focused on three features: Web & App Activity, Location History, and Location Accuracy. Regulators found Google did not process location data lawfully, fairly, or transparently, and kept some data longer than necessary. Users may not have known their location information could influence advertising or reveal their interests.

Google must bring its processing into compliance within six months. The company said the case concerns historical policies that have since been updated and that it has added more user controls. The probe began after complaints from European consumer groups, including BEUC. This is the fourth largest fine from the Irish regulator, which oversees Google because its EU headquarters are in Dublin. The full decision will be published separately.

stories.Headline: Vyzoxa Redefines AI Learning Through Practical AI Agent Development, Empowering Learners Worldwide to Build With Artificial Intelligence
stories.Summary:
Vyzoxa, an education technology platform run by NDFM Business World Pvt. Ltd., has announced a new learning pathway focused on building AI agents rather than just studying artificial intelligence. The company, based in Amritsar, India, aims to help create one million AI innovators by 2030. Its program includes about two weeks of industrial training followed by a four-week project internship in AI agent development at no extra cost. Learners use integrated tools called Vyzoxa Intelligent Systems, including an AI mentor, AI coder, and AI engine, to support their work.

The remote, self-paced program is open to eligible participants in India and international markets such as North America, Europe, Asia, the Middle East, Africa, and Asia-Pacific. Founder Mansajan Singh and Managing Director Gurjinder Singh lead the effort. After completing the project, top performers enrolled from India may be shortlisted for a final interview and could progress to employment or pre-placement offers, though these opportunities are not guaranteed. International participants can take the learning pathway, but job and pre-placement offers currently apply only to India.

stories.Headline: Australia AI regulations: Anthropic, OpenAI call for Australia to relax ban on training of AI models
stories.Summary:
OpenAI and Anthropic have asked Australia to soften its planned ban on using local creative content to train artificial intelligence models. The two US companies made submissions to a parliamentary inquiry in September, arguing that a narrow copyright exemption could protect creators while attracting investment. Australia has already ruled out such an exemption, and its broader AI and data centre rules take effect next year. The companies say the sector could be worth hundreds of billions of dollars by the end of the decade.

Anthropic proposed a conditional approval system and said it would consider conditions that support Australian creators. OpenAI called for a balanced framework allowing models to learn from information that is publicly available while giving rightsholders chances to collaborate. Both companies linked their requests to major local projects, including an OpenAI data centre deal in Sydney and an Anthropic partnership in Queensland. The Joint Select Committee on Artificial Intelligence is due to report in November.

stories.Headline: Trump Wants To Rename AI 'Super Intelligence', Calling 'Artificial' Inaccurate as He Plans AI Force and Czar
stories.Summary:
President Donald Trump proposed renaming artificial intelligence as "Super Intelligence," calling "artificial" inaccurate and inelegant. In Truth Social posts on 19 and 21 September 2026, he polled followers on names like Superior Intelligence and Extreme Intelligence. Superior Intelligence reportedly led with 41.5 percent, though the sample was not representative. Trump then adopted Super Intelligence, or SI. The article notes superintelligence already describes a hypothetical future intellect far beyond humans, so this is a rebranding, not a technical change.

Trump also announced an AI Force, similar to the Space Force, and said he would soon name an AI Czar, with only high IQ individuals eligible. No structure, funding, or authority was detailed, leaving its role unclear. He tied the plan to staying ahead of China and downplayed safety warnings. A Reuters/Ipsos poll found 73 percent of 1,277 US adults think AI companies are not doing enough to prevent harm. For now, artificial intelligence remains the standard term, and the AI Force is only a proposal with no defined next steps.

stories.Headline: OpenAI Launches Math Advisory Group as AI Advances Mathematical Research With 100+ Solutions
stories.Summary:
OpenAI has created an independent math advisory group hosted at the Institute for Advanced Study in Princeton. It includes nine mathematicians, such as Timothy Gowers and Edward Witten, who will not be paid and can make recommendations public. The group will review AI-generated mathematical results, assess their importance, and help share them with the wider math community, but it will not advise on the speed of OpenAI's internal research.

The company says a new internal model that began training on August 28 has resolved more than 100 long-standing open problems across most areas of mathematics, and it links this work to a claimed solution of the Navier-Stokes Millennium Prize problem. This follows 10 results published in August. The advisory group is expected to provide independent input as OpenAI continues developing AI systems for mathematical research.

stories.Headline: Gov. Hochul Says New York’s New AI Compliance Office Could Explore ‘Kill Switch’ - Insurance Journal
stories.Summary:
New York Governor Kathy Hochul is launching a state office to monitor safety compliance for large artificial intelligence companies. She appointed Marc Gilman, an attorney at the Department of Financial Services, to lead the new Digital Innovation, Governance, Integrity and Trust office, created by the RAISE Act signed in December 2025. The law sets some of the strongest US restrictions on major AI developers such as OpenAI and Anthropic. Hochul said future safeguards could include an AI kill switch if it is feasible and beneficial, echoing a similar proposal from California Governor Gavin Newsom.

Under the RAISE Act, large developers must register in November, and enforcement begins in January. They must publish safety protocols and report critical incidents within 72 hours or face civil penalties. Hochul criticized the Trump administration for not regulating AI nationally, saying states must fill the gap. Gilman previously worked as general counsel and compliance vice president at software firm Theta Lake. The article does not specify further steps beyond exploring the kill switch idea.

stories.Headline: Menendez bills to fight AI-driven cyberattacks, protect from scams, clears committee - Hudson County View
stories.Summary:
Two bills from U.S. Representative Rob Menendez of New Jersey's 8th District passed the House Energy and Commerce Committee. The AI For Secure Networks Act, co-sponsored by Representative August Pfluger of Texas, aims to strengthen cybersecurity for communications networks by encouraging responsible artificial intelligence use and reducing risks from AI-driven attacks. It passed unanimously by a 37 to 0 vote. Menendez said the measure protects communications, emergency services, critical infrastructure, and financial systems.

The second bill, the Strategic Task Force on Scam Prevention Act, co-sponsored by Representative Erin Houchin of Indiana, creates a federal task force to build a national scam prevention strategy. It would improve victim support, give local police stronger tools, and lower financial losses from fraud. This bill cleared the committee unanimously by a 36 to 0 vote. Menendez said it is one step closer to becoming law and he looks forward to House passage.
